headline: Speaking more languages may keep the brain younger

sources.title: Speaking multiple languages may slow brain aging by years, study finds
Multilingualism Subtracts Up to 13 Years from Brain Age
Speaking another language could slow aging in the brain
Study shows learning another language appears to slow brain aging (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} [[a new way to]] measure how quickly the human brain grows older. At a large science [[conference]] in Europe, a research team from the Basque region of Spain {{pointed out}} that people who speak several languages often have younger brains than their [[chronological]] age would suggest. The team {{set out}} to test [[whether]] knowing more than one language can [[slow]] this kind of [[aging]]. Their [[early results]] suggest that it can.

verbs.correct: To think of or create a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To face a problem you did not expect
verbs.why: Teams come up with new plans when the old one fails, and kids come up with clever excuses for being late. Scientists came up with a new way to measure how quickly a person's brain is aging.

verbs.correct: To tell people a fact they may not have noticed
verbs.wrong: To prove that something is completely true
verbs.why: A good editor points out small mistakes before a piece is published, and a friend might point out a detail you missed completely. Researchers pointed out that people who speak several languages often have younger looking brains.

verbs.correct: To begin doing something with a clear goal in mind
verbs.wrong: To hope strongly for a particular result
verbs.why: A runner sets out to break a personal record, and a young company sets out to change how people shop. This research team set out to test whether speaking more languages could slow brain aging.

chunks.text: The researchers used [[a form of]] artificial intelligence to {{work out}} each person's 'brain age' from [[patterns]] of brain [[connectivity]]. They looked at 144 people in the Basque region who spoke between one and four languages, such as Spanish, Basque, French, and English. As the number of languages grew, the brains [[appeared]] younger and younger. People who spoke two languages had brains that seemed about six years younger, while those who spoke four {{ended up}} with brains that looked around thirteen years younger.

verbs.correct: To calculate or figure something out
verbs.wrong: To guess an answer without any real evidence
verbs.why: Friends work out a fair way to split a bill, and a student might work out the answer in her head before checking it. Researchers used artificial intelligence to work out each person's brain age from patterns in the brain.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a certain result or state
verbs.wrong: To improve step by step over many years
verbs.why: You end up lost on a new street sometimes, or you end up with the last slice of pizza nobody else wanted. People who spoke four languages in this study ended up with brains that looked about thirteen years younger.

chunks.text: The scientists say the number of languages is not the only thing that {{stands out}}. People who {{picked up}} a second language early in life, and who reached [[a high level of]] [[proficiency]], seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly. Being truly [[fluent]] appeared to matter [[just as much as]] speaking many languages. Constantly [[switching between]] languages may give the brain a kind of daily workout that keeps it healthy.

verbs.correct: To be clearly noticed as important
verbs.wrong: To be the main cause of a result
verbs.why: One answer can stand out as clearly the best in an interview, and good manners often stand out in a crowded room. In this research, the number of languages a person speaks is not the only factor that stands out.

verbs.correct: To learn a skill or language informally
verbs.wrong: To formally study a subject in a class
verbs.why: Children pick up new words just by listening, and travelers often pick up a bit of the local language after a few weeks abroad. People in this study who picked up a second language early in life kept more of the brain benefit.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose or give it up
verbs.wrong: To gain even more of something over time
verbs.why: People hold on to old photos for years, and a worker might hold on to a steady job through hard times. Early, fluent language speakers in this study seemed to hold on to the brain benefit more strongly than others.

chunks.text: These [[findings]] match a much larger project that {{looked into}} the health of 86,149 older people across 27 European countries. In that [[survey]], people who spoke several languages were about [[half as likely]] to show fast, unhealthy aging. Experts say the two studies {{back up}} a simple message: it is [[never too late]] to start. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow some of the mental [[decline]] that often [[comes with age]].

verbs.correct: To examine or investigate something carefully
verbs.wrong: To protect and be responsible for something
verbs.why: Doctors look into the cause of an illness, and a shopper might look into cheaper flights before booking a trip. A separate, much larger project looked into the health of more than 86,000 older adults across Europe.

verbs.correct: To support something and show that it is true
verbs.wrong: To give a short summary of the main points
verbs.why: New evidence can back up an old theory, and test results sometimes back up exactly what a doctor already suspected. Experts say these two language studies back up a simple message: it is never too late to start.

verbs.correct: To start doing a new activity, hobby, or study
verbs.wrong: To fill or use a large amount of time or space
verbs.why: Adults take up gardening after retirement, and some people take up running to relieve stress. Adults who take up a new language later in life may still slow some of the mental decline that often happens with age.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that people who speak more languages often have brains that look younger. A larger study of older adults across Europe backed up the same finding.
mainIdea.why: The team found brains looked years younger with each added language, and a larger survey of 86,149 people across 27 countries backed up the finding.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that the number of languages a person speaks matters more than anything else. Adults who took up a new language late in life got the strongest results.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the story says early fluency mattered just as much as the number of languages, not more than everything else.

mainIdea.s: A separate team in Asia studied how regular exercise affects memory in older adults. Their results suggest that daily walks may lower the risk of memory loss as people age.
mainIdea.why: This story is about researchers linking multiple languages to slower brain aging, not a study on exercise and memory.

tf.s: The team set out to test whether knowing more than one language can slow brain aging.
tf.why: Correct. The researchers set out to test whether speaking several languages slows this kind of aging.

tf.s: People who spoke four languages ended up with brains that looked older than their real age.
tf.why: They ended up with brains that looked about thirteen years younger, not older.

tf.s: The scientists came up with a way to make people speak more languages instantly.
tf.why: They came up with a way to measure brain age, not a way to make people speak languages instantly.

tf.s: Experts say the two studies back up the idea that it is never too late to learn a language.
tf.why: The story says the studies back up the message that it is never too late to start.

tf.s: A larger project looked into the health of 86,149 people across 27 European countries.
tf.why: The bigger survey looked into the health of 86,149 older people in 27 European countries.

tf.s: The study found that people who picked up a second language early got fewer benefits.
tf.why: People who picked up a second language early and became fluent held on to the benefit more strongly, so they got more, not fewer, benefits.

lines.text: [[Good news for you]]. Scientists say speaking more languages may keep your brain younger.
Really? So my three languages are good for something?
Very good. Researchers in Spain {{came up with}} a way to measure "brain age" and {{set out}} to test whether languages slow aging.
How do you measure a brain's age?
With AI. It can {{work out}} your brain age from connection patterns. They tested 144 people who spoke one to four languages.
The more languages, the younger the brain. Two languages looked about six years younger. People with four {{ended up}} with brains around thirteen years younger.
The scientists {{pointed out}} that fluency matters too. People who {{picked up}} a second language early and reached a high level seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly.
A bigger project {{looked into}} the health of 86,000 older people across Europe, and it {{backs up}} the same message. Multilinguals were half as likely to show fast aging.
Never. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow the decline that comes with age.
